claims.text: The preserved source names a dynamic-programming stock best-time family with basic, unlimited and N-limited variants but does not preserve exact APIs or detailed trade constraints.
Under the explicit candidate contract, the one/unlimited/at-most-k implementations are exhaustively equivalent to legal buy/sell/skip state search on the bounded oracle domain.
The fixture verifies rising/falling/empty/singleton/large-k and invalid-input boundaries plus exhaustive arrays length 0..6 over prices 0..3 for k=0..4.

findings: The preserved source asks for the stock best-time family solved with dynamic programming and names basic, unlimited and N-limited variants, but does not preserve exact APIs or detailed trading rules.

The candidate explicitly labels non-negative prices, one-share holding, no fee/cooldown/shorting, basic=at-most-one and N-limited=at-most-k as answer-side assumptions instead of recovered source facts.

The one-transaction recurrence prevents a post-sale second purchase; the unlimited recurrence uses prior-day cash/hold; the at-most-k recurrence uses oldSell[t-1] -> buy[t] and oldBuy[t] -> sell[t], matching the declared completed-transaction layering.
The k>=floor(n/2) shortcut is valid under the declared no-fee/no-cooldown/one-share contract and is not generalized to unpreserved variants.

The displayed Java class compiles and the deterministic fixture checks 5461 arrays of length 0..6 over prices 0..3 against an independent exhaustive buy/sell/skip oracle for one, unlimited and k=0..4, plus named and invalid-input boundaries.
Complexity, initialization, no-trade behavior and missing-source boundaries are explained; no fabricated project experience, source attribution, placeholder code or coding hard failure remains.
Formal promotion remains subject to repository promotion and real-review policy.
